questions.heading: Trap Questions: Prices and Conflicts That Promise Too Much
questions.stem: In an LP's report, the crew row of 2029 has slack 0 and a dual value of 0 at the optimum. How should the report label it?

options.text: Binding with a zero price, since binding means zero slack alone
options.says: Right: a degenerate vertex can bind a row and put its price on other rows; report slack and price separately.

options.text: Not binding, since a binding row must also carry a nonzero price
options.says: That is the study-guide definition the trap corrects; the printed LP has a binding row with price 0.

options.text: Not binding, since a zero price shows the row still has room left
options.says: Slack 0 means the row has no room left; the price says nothing about room.

options.text: An error, since a row with no slack must carry a nonzero price
options.says: GLOP returned exactly this at OPTIMAL on the degenerate LP; it is degeneracy, not an error.

questions.heading: Trap Questions: Prices and Conflicts That Promise Too Much
questions.stem: You fix a capital plan's binaries at their values and re-solve the LP; the 2029 budget row's dual value is 1.25. Finance asks what $50k more in 2029 would buy. What do you answer?

options.text: $62.5k of NPV, since the next $1k is worth the same whatever the budget
options.says: The MILP's value is a step function: the next $1k buys nothing at most budgets and a whole step at a few.

options.text: Nothing, since a budget row that binds carries a price of zero
options.says: Binding means zero slack; the printed degenerate LP has binding rows priced at 1, and this row's dual is 1.25.

options.text: Unknown without a new run, since the price is local to this one plan
options.says: Right: with more money the plan may change; the MILP's value moves in steps, so re-solve the MILP.

options.text: $62.5k of NPV, since a MILP's value rises at the budget's shadow price
options.says: A MILP has no shadow prices; its value is a step function of the budget.

questions.heading: Round 1: A Failed Scenario Gets a Status, a Conflict and a Repair
questions.stem: A scenario's rules are listed R1 to R6, and it has two conflicts: {R1, R2} and {R4, R5, R6}. A deletion filter tests the rules in that order. Which conflict does it report?

options.text: {R1, R2}, since the filter reports the first conflict it meets
options.says: Testing R1 first finds the rest still infeasible, so R1 and then R2 are dropped.

options.text: {R4, R5, R6}, since the filter keeps the conflict it tests last
options.says: Right: rules are dropped while the rest stays infeasible, so the conflict listed last survives.

options.text: Both, since the filter keeps each row that is part of a conflict
options.says: A deletion filter returns one conflict, irreducible: no row can be dropped from it.

options.text: {R1, R2}, since the filter prefers the smallest conflict it finds
options.says: An IIS is irreducible, not the smallest; the order decides which one is kept.
